This is substantively equivalent — same objective of defending against fine-tuning-based jailbreaks with minimal toxic examples.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: using safety probes to locate attention heads most correlated with harmfulness, determining a "safety direction" per head, injecting intervention vectors at inference time to push activations toward harmlessness, with multi-token dimension search for robustness/transferability.

- Paper [24] "Inference-Time Intervention (ITI)" introduces shifting model activations during inference "following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads" — this is the core primitive: probe attention heads, find directions, inject at inference time.
- Paper [23] "Non-Linear ITI (NL-ITI)" extends ITI with "non-linear multi-token probing and multi-token intervention" — directly matching the multi-token dimension search aspect.

The evaluation design (ASR measurement on harmful instruction benchmarks, jailbreak attack success rates) is well-covered by multiple prior papers, particularly [6], [4], [5].

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable safety interventions to be extracted once from a base model and distributed across multiple fine-tuned variants, avoiding repeated searches for safety patterns. Paper [1] discusses safety risks associated with fine-tuning aligned LLMs but does not propose a method to extract and distribute safety interventions across variants. Paper [3] introduces "Antidote," which defends against harmful fine-tuning but does not address the extraction and distribution of safety interventions. Paper [6] explores bias mitigation effects in fine-tuning but focuses on transferability of bias reduction rather than safety intervention extraction and distribution. None of the prior papers explicitly address the same objective.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves extracting safety bias directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from a base model's activations and universally applying them to fine-tuned models based on the finding that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations. Paper [8] introduces "Contrastive Activation Addition" (CAA), which computes steering vectors from residual stream activations to modify model behavior during inference. Paper [23] explores extracting latent steering vectors from pretrained models for controllable text generation. Paper [22] rigorously investigates the generalization and reliability of steering vectors across tasks and distributions. Both papers use similar evaluation designs (activation-based steering applied across models and tasks), making the evaluation facet covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of transferable safety alignment for large language models (LLMs). Paper [1] addresses safety alignment risks in fine-tuned LLMs, and Paper [3] proposes defenses against harmful fine-tuning attacks. Paper [8] and Paper [22] focus on steering vectors for modifying LLM behavior, which includes safety-related applications. All these papers operate in the general domain of LLM safety alignment, making the domain facet covered.
